The FTC's amended COPPA rule reached its full compliance date on 22 Apr 2026, civil penalties can reach about 53,000 USD per violation, and Disney paid 10M USD in Sep 2025 for relying on channel level labels, so every Bro Bros upload should be marked made for kids video by video, not only at channel level.

YouTube's machine learning can switch a video to 'made for kids' on its own, and once that label is set the creator cannot change it back without an appeal, so any non kids content we ever post (behind the scenes, adult tutorials) belongs on a separate channel.

The FTC decides whether content is child directed from its subject, visuals, animated characters, music, language, the ages of people shown and audience data, and a video does not count just because some children watch it, so our animated, song led videos are clearly made for kids and must carry that label on YouTube.

A simple self check from 2026 AI crackdown guides: if anyone else could produce the same video from the same prompt, the video is at risk under YouTube's inauthentic content rule, so each Bro Bros song needs its own human made choices (a story, a joke, a named dance, a scene) that a prompt alone would not give.

The channels removed in YouTube's 2026 AI cleanup had no human editorial step at all (AI wrote, voiced, animated and uploaded), and guides now advise auditing the last 20 to 30 uploads for repeated structure; for Bro Bros that means checking every week that titles, scenes and dance moves are not copies of last week's with a new name.

Getting into the YouTube Kids app starts with a family friendly classification, then automated filters that check the thumbnail, the title and the video itself, so one scary thumbnail or a rude word in a title can block a whole song from the app.
leaves.src: PPC Land citing YouTube Kids FAQ, Apr 2026

leaves.t: YouTube Kids excludes videos built around product packaging or piling up and consuming lots of products, and any paid placement, so Bro Bros toy, gift or present songs should show play and kindness, not unboxing hauls.
leaves.src: PPC Land citing YouTube Kids FAQ, Apr 2026

leaves.t: Parent flagged videos in YouTube Kids are reviewed around the clock and removed for all users if found unsuitable, so a single upsetting scene (a scary monster, a fall or a fight) can cost a song its YouTube Kids reach everywhere.
leaves.src: PPC Land citing YouTube Kids FAQ, Apr 2026

leaves.t: US regulators now treat autoplay, recommendations, notifications and public comments as possible harms to children, and the FTC's 2025 10M USD Disney case was about kids videos labelled 'not made for kids', so every Bro Bros upload must be set to made for kids.

After the 2020 made for kids change, kids channels cut uploads about 18%, original content fell 11% and manual captions 27%, and viewer ratings fell 10%, so careful original songs with real captions now stand out among kids uploads.
leaves.src: Johnson, Lin, Cooper and Zhong, AEA 2025 conference paper

leaves.t: Instagram teen accounts can no longer follow or see accounts that regularly post age inappropriate content, so a single risky stunt, rude word or scary clip on our Instagram could cut us off from older siblings and teen viewers; keep every Reel fully family safe.

The teen 'door kick challenge' (kicking or banging on strangers' doors at night, filming and running away) spread across the US and UK and led to police reports and arrests, so Bro Bros visit and surprise formats must always show a friendly ring at a family member's door that is answered, never knocking at strangers' houses or running away.

YouTube Kids relies on automated checks of thumbnail, title and video plus spot human review (it cannot review every video), and parent reports are checked around the clock; a video judged unsuitable is removed for all users, so one scary or rude frame can take a Bro Bros song out of the app entirely.
leaves.src: PPC Land / YouTube Help FAQ, Apr 2026

leaves.t: AIR's growth cases repeatedly start with a cleanup: removing kids videos that sit close to policy limits (clickbait thumbnails, frightening or low quality scenes) before pushing new uploads, which suggests one weak or borderline video can hold back a whole kids channel's recommendations.

Among the Spanish language channels YouTube removed in late January 2026 was Cuentos Fascinantes (over 5.9M subscribers, about 1.2B views), which posted AI made stories using a famous anime franchise's characters, proof that size gives no protection when a channel is mass produced and leans on protected characters.

TNW (Jun 2026) reports that YouTube judges inauthentic content at channel level and a pattern across a channel's recent uploads can switch off monetisation for every video, so Bro Bros must keep each of the 14 weekly songs visibly different (new melody, new set, new dance, new story beat) rather than one template with swapped words.

Faceless creators report heavier demonetisation in 2026 and some now add an on screen human host to prove human craft; for an animated kids channel the safer equivalent is showing the human work openly, such as a short behind the scenes Short of the owner building a Blender scene or choreographing a dance.

A TikTok creator's viral 2024 dance was sold as a Roblox emote about 60,000 times (at least about 123K USD) before a licence was agreed and she sued in April 2025, citing past choreography copyright claims, so Bro Bros must invent its own dance moves and never copy a named creator's exact routine step for step.

The European Commission adopted the Digital Fairness Act proposal on 11 Nov 2026: any trader (not just platforms) would be barred from profiling based ads to consumers known to be minors, influencers could not directly urge minors to buy or hide paid deals, and services that encourage compulsive use must offer switches to turn off autoplay and endless scrolling; it still needs Parliament and Council approval and would apply 12 months after entry into force.

For Bro Bros the Digital Fairness Act means never telling kids in a song or caption to buy or ask for a product, labelling any future brand deal as 'advertisement', and expecting EU fines of up to 6% of turnover to push platforms toward even stricter kids ad rules from 2028.

In AIR's 300 channel study kids channels' RPM rose about 22% in Q4 versus the rest of the year (behind food and crafts, level with music), while all format RPM dropped from about 2.12 USD in December to 1.56 USD in January, so December is the month to have the most kids videos live and January needs cheaper, evergreen uploads.

Brazil's federal prosecutors opened an inquiry into Kwai in Jan 2024 after reporters found children being harassed in its live streams and weak moderation, so if Bro Bros ever posts on Kwai for Brazil it should use pre recorded videos only, never lives, and watch brand safety closely.

The same 12 Nov 2026 report reminds parents that YouTube admits not every YouTube Kids video is reviewed by a person, which keeps parent trust as the deciding factor; a channel description and pinned playlist that state plainly what each song teaches gives worried parents a reason to pick us.

vidIQ's 2026 CPM guide shows US ad prices rising from about 1.8 USD in August to about 5.7 USD in December, spiking near 6.9 USD in Cyber Week (late November), then falling 30 to 50% by late February, so Bro Bros' best songs of the year should be live and monetisable before Thanksgiving week, not only before Christmas.

vidIQ puts made for kids CPMs at about 1 to 4 USD against 8 to 20 USD or more for similar adult content, and India at only 0.5 to 3 USD against 10 to 30 USD or more for the US, which is why our English songs aimed at US, UK, Canada and Australia carry most of the revenue potential.

The FTC's 2026 actions touching children and AI so far hit chatbots (a 6(b) inquiry), an AI 'active listening' ad service and a robot toy maker (500,000 USD), not animated video channels, so for Bro Bros the live US risk remains correct made for kids labels on every video rather than our AI assisted production.
leaves.src: Privacy + Security Forum FTC update, Nov 2026

leaves.t: Meta agreed in late Aug 2026 to a proposed settlement of up to about 17.1B USD with 50 US states, territories and DC: under 18 users get a default 2 hour daily limit only a parent can lift, an overnight block (reported as midnight or 10 PM to 6 AM), no notifications in school hours (8 AM to 3 PM) and hidden like counts, and Meta is pressing TikTok and YouTube to match.

New York's law requiring a mental health warning label on platforms with addictive features (algorithmic feeds, autoplay, infinite scroll, like counts, push notifications) takes effect on 1 Jan 2027 unless blocked; NetChoice, whose members include YouTube, Instagram and TikTok, sued on 17 Nov 2026 on free speech grounds.

With California's AB 1709 (from 1 Jan 2027, fines up to 50K USD per child) and New York's labels both aimed at feeds and autoplay for minors, US discovery for under 16s may lean more on search, subscriptions and parent chosen playlists in 2027, so clear searchable titles and strong playlists are the safe bet for Bro Bros.

vidIQ's newer model puts Kidshire's ad income at only about 13K USD for 28 days of about 545M views (roughly 0.02 to 0.03 USD per 1,000), while its older page model gave a similar Shorts channel (Toys and Colors Shorts, about 357M views a month in Apr 2025) 0.65M to 2M USD a month, so vidIQ income estimates for kids Shorts disagree wildly; the safe lesson is that Shorts pay far less per view than long videos, so Bro Bros should use Shorts for discovery and earn mainly from long videos and compilations.

UK broadcast rules (Ofcom flashing images guidance, followed in Japan too) fail any sequence with more than three flashes in one second covering over a quarter of the screen, treat any sudden change to or from saturated red as harmful whatever its brightness, and say flashing that lasts longer than 5 seconds can be risky even inside the limits, so Bro Bros fireworks, disco lights and star sparkles should pulse at most 3 times a second, stay small on screen and avoid full screen red flashes.

The same guidance treats regular striped patterns with more than five light and dark pairs as risky (still stripes over 40% of the screen, or moving, flickering stripes over 25%), while stripes that flow smoothly in one direction are fine, so striped backgrounds, zebra crossings and candy cane walls should be kept small or scroll smoothly rather than flicker.

Photosensitive epilepsy affects roughly 1 in 4,000 people and became a children's TV issue after a 1997 Japanese cartoon's bright red flashes sent hundreds of children to hospital; US broadcasters and online platforms do not pre test for it, so a kids channel has to check its own flashy scenes, which also keeps them ready for TV or streaming sales later.

Vietnam's draft amendment to Decree 147 (Sept 2026, not yet adopted) does not ban under 16s but makes a parent register and supervise every under 16 social account with the parent's own phone or ID, locks posting, commenting, sharing and reactions for under 13s on large foreign platforms, and requires any channel or page with 1M+ followers to file contact details with the ministry, so Vietnamese viewing of kids songs will run through parent accounts and a future Bro Bros at 1M followers would need to register there.

The European Commission must publish its evaluation of the Audiovisual Media Services Directive by 19 Dec 2026, and the options under review range from no change to targeted rules for influencers and short form video creators or a full EU content regulation, with protection of young viewers online named as a focus; any new duties for channels like Bro Bros would come after 2027, but EU audiences may later bring TV style rules on kids content and advertising to YouTube creators.

California's Digital Age Assurance Act (AB 1043) takes effect on 1 Jan 2027: device makers must ask a user's age when a device account is set up (a parent enters it for under 18s) and send apps an age bracket signal (under 13, 13 to 15, 16 to 17, 18+), and apps must request that signal and treat it as actual knowledge of age, so from 2027 apps like YouTube and Instagram will know far more reliably which Californian viewers are children, pushing them into child settings where personalised ads and comments are off.

Google withholds US tax only from YouTube earnings made from US viewers if the creator files Form W-8BEN in AdSense (India's treaty rate is 15%, entered with the PAN and the 'other copyright royalties' line), but can withhold up to 24% of all worldwide YouTube earnings if no form is filed, so the Bro Bros AdSense account needs an approved W-8BEN before the first payout.

A W-8BEN signed in 2026 stays valid until 31 Dec 2029, Google asks creators to review tax info by 10 December each year, and wrongly withheld tax can only be refunded within the same calendar year (corrected form by 31 Dec), so checking the Bro Bros tax form in early December matters this year.

An Oct 2026 ESRB Privacy Certified analysis notes that US states now attack kids' harms mainly through design rules (recommendation feeds, push notifications, time limits) while COPPA covers data, and repeats that the FTC's Disney case punished child directed YouTube videos marked 'not made for kids'; marking every Bro Bros upload made for kids stays the safest choice.

YouTube's coming voice comments by TV remote (only when the same account is signed in on TV and phone) do nothing for Bro Bros, because comments are switched off on made for kids videos; our TV engagement signals stay watch time, rewatches and session length.

Ofcom reported on 24 Oct 2026 that the share of UK children aged 8 to 17 seeing harmful content had not changed in the nine months after its child safety duties began (July 2025) and said platforms must go 'much further and faster', so expect tighter recommendation rules for young viewers in 2027 that favour clearly gentle, made for kids content like ours.

The UK's spring 2027 package bans under 16s from livestreaming on every platform and blocks unknown adults from contacting children, while watching streams stays allowed, so a Bro Bros 24/7 music stream is unaffected as long as it never invites children to appear or chat.

A New York Times investigation (Feb 2026) found that after one CoComelon or 'Wheels on the Bus' video, over 40% of the Shorts YouTube recommended in a 15 minute session had AI made visuals, all under 30 seconds and often with warped faces, extra limbs and garbled text; YouTube then removed the five cited channels from the Partner Program and from YouTube Kids.

Since YouTube's AI disclosure label is required for realistic synthetic content but not for animated kids videos, the line between 'AI tool assisted' and 'AI slop' is judged by quality: Bro Bros must keep the same character models every time, check every frame for glitches (warped hands, extra limbs, garbled on screen text) and give each song a real learning or play purpose, because slop channels are being cut off from earnings and YouTube Kids.

YouTube's answer to the 200 plus groups asking it to ban AI kids videos is that AI made content on YouTube Kids is limited to a smaller set of vetted channels, AI use must be disclosed, and mass produced spammy uploads are penalised; to stay eligible for YouTube Kids, Bro Bros should disclose AI music and motion honestly and show clear human creative direction in every video.

In January 2026 YouTube terminated 16 channels with about 35M subscribers and 4.7B views under its renamed 'inauthentic content' policy, and review looks at a channel's pattern across recent uploads, so one templated, look alike stretch of videos can demonetise the whole channel, not just those videos; vary songs, scenes and formats week to week.

YouTube says AI labelled videos are not penalised in recommendations or monetisation as long as there is real human creative input; the crackdown hits faceless channels pumping out the same template, even ones not using AI, so original songs, named recurring characters and visible behind the scenes human work protect Bro Bros.

Texas filed House Bill 212 in November 2026 for the January 2027 session: it would bar under 16s from social media accounts even with parental permission, require age checks before sign up and let parents ask for removal within 10 days; if passed it starts 1 Sep 2027 with the restrictions from 1 Jan 2028, and it names Instagram, TikTok, Facebook and X but not YouTube.

Because the US under 16 bills (like Texas HB 212) target account holders, Bro Bros should keep speaking to parents on Instagram (captions and Reels written for mums and dads) and keep YouTube as the main home for kids, which none of these bills names.

From 18 Nov 2026 Google's AI Ultra plans include YouTube Premium Family (ad free YouTube and YouTube Music for up to six people in a household), so more family TVs will play Bro Bros without ads, which makes total watch time, not only ad views, matter for earnings.

YouTube removed BabyBus's 'Super JoJo' channel (about 22M subscribers, one of the 25 biggest animation channels) in August 2021 after multiple third party copyright claims, when Moonbug sued over copied CoComelon characters, settings, song titles, lyrics and images; in August 2023 a US court awarded Moonbug about 23.4M US dollars against BabyBus.
leaves.src: Cartoon Brew Sep 2021 and Senal News Aug 2023

leaves.t: One of the copied videos cited against Super JoJo was a 'boo boo' song, so when Bro Bros covers a common preschool topic that a giant already owns (boo boos, bath time, yes yes vegetables) we must use our own title wording, our own melody and lyrics and our own scene ideas, never a lookalike of the leader's version.

As quoted in November 2026, YouTube's monetization page accepts a series that follows a set of characters with 'a distinct storyline, focus, or concept' and content showing a unique creative voice, but refuses videos showing 'the same situation over and over again with the same outcome' and AI content made from generic templates, so each Bro Bros song must have its own situation and its own ending, not just new lyrics on the same dance scene.

YouTube's child safety policy removes 'misleading family content', meaning kid styled videos (cartoon look, kids title or tags, made for kids setting) that carry mature themes such as violence, scary adult horror characters, medical procedures or self harm, with warnings and strikes and termination after three strikes in 90 days, so Bro Bros keeps doctor, monster or Halloween themes gentle and clearly playful.

YouTube's quality principles for kids content list 'strange use of children's characters' as a low quality sign that can limit ads, and a channel strongly focused on low quality made for kids videos can be suspended from the Partner Program, so odd or random mash ups of characters should never appear in Bro Bros videos.

YouTube's August 2026 update sends 60% of net Premium Lite subscription revenue into a creator pool split by how much members watch each channel, so as Lite spreads to every Premium country, minutes watched by ad free families also pay Bro Bros, not only ad views.

The Feb 2027 Partner Program bar (8,000 watch hours or 20M Shorts views) applies only to new applicants, while the lower entry tier for fan funding and shopping stays the same; that lower tier gives little to Bro Bros because memberships, Super Chat and Super Thanks are switched off on made for kids videos, so full ad revenue sharing is the real goal.

YouTube reported more than 200 billion Shorts views a day in August 2026, so the 20M Shorts views in 90 days route into the Partner Program is a tiny slice of the feed; one breakout kids Short can carry a new channel past it faster than 8,000 watch hours of long songs.

YouTube Kids only shows pre approved ads and bans food and drink, beauty, dating and political ads, with non skippable ads of 15 to 20 seconds, which is one reason kids video ad rates stay below general audience rates.
leaves.src: Broadcast Media Africa (YouTube Kids at 10), Sep 2025

leaves.t: An August 2026 settlement between a group of US states and Meta requires Meta to detect and remove users under 13 with an age prediction model, so kids reaching our Instagram Reels directly will shrink further; our Reels should speak to parents (the account is run by an adult for families) while the songs themselves stay for children.

State attorneys general in the US increasingly pursue kids' harms under their own consumer protection and privacy laws rather than COPPA, because 'directed to children' is hard to prove, so a clearly kids directed channel like ours is safest by labelling every video made for kids and leaving comments and personalised ads off as YouTube already enforces.

Several Indonesian kids song channels put a famous protected train character's name in titles of their own train songs to catch search (one such compilation has about 180M views), a shortcut that risks claims and misleading metadata strikes; Bro Bros train songs should use only our own vehicle names.

From 1 Feb 2027 new channels can join the YouTube Partner Program only with 8,000 qualified watch hours in the last 365 days or 20 million qualified Shorts views in the last 90 days (double today's bars); channels already in the programme are not affected, so Bro Bros should aim to qualify before February under the current, lower bar.

Also from 1 Feb 2027 a channel keeps earning from Shorts ads only while it has 10 million qualified Shorts views in the last rolling 90 days; below that it still earns on long videos and Shorts money returns automatically once it crosses 10M again, so for a young kids channel the long songs are the dependable income and Shorts are mainly for discovery.

YouTube's 2027 revenue split stays 55% to the creator for long form ads and 45% for Shorts, and Premium Lite (with a 60% creator pool) expands to every Premium country, so watch time on long songs and compilations is worth more per view than Shorts views.

Cartoon Brew says the new rolling 10M Shorts bar favours channels that can turn out lots of Shorts quickly and pushes slower hand animators toward long form; one creator estimated 9M qualified Shorts views earned only about 2,600 US dollars, so Shorts income alone would not fund our 14 songs a week.

Bloomberg reported that channels linked to Animaj, the AI kids studio Google backed in March 2026 (about 1M USD from its AI Futures Fund), including the infant channel Hey Kids with over 4M subscribers, gained more than 22 billion views in 2025, so AI assisted kids studios already compete at the very top of baby and toddler YouTube.

The same deal gives Animaj exclusive early access to Google's generative video tools, which means AI made preschool videos will get cheaper and more common, so Bro Bros must stand out on original songs, recurring characters and real story variety rather than on volume.

Denmark's planned under 15 social media ban comes with an official age verification app, and parents could let children from 13 join after an assessment, so in Denmark (as in Australia) young viewers will reach our videos mainly through logged out, parent or YouTube Kids viewing.

New Zealand's Social Media (Age-Restricted Users) Bill, proposed by the Prime Minister on 24 Aug 2026 with fines up to 10% of turnover and still pushed by both main parties in Nov 2026, and a Kazakhstan draft law (2026) that may cover YouTube and TikTok, would join Australia, Indonesia and the UK in banning under 16 accounts, so more of our viewers will watch through YouTube Kids, logged out TV viewing or a parent's account and our titles and captions must keep speaking to the parent who presses play.
leaves.src: The Spinoff, Tengrinews, WSWS, Aug to Nov 2026

leaves.t: South Dakota sued TikTok in state court on 19 Nov 2026 alleging harm to minors after federal settlement talks stalled, another sign that US states keep tightening kids' social media, which favours made for kids content on YouTube over TikTok for our audience.

A Finnish study following 260 children for eight years (Pediatric Exercise Science, reported 17 Nov 2026) linked more childhood screen time to better cognitive processing at about 16 and less unsupervised time to better results, so parents' worry is shifting from minutes to what is watched and with whom, which favours calm co viewable songs.

Instagram's stricter 'Limited Content' setting, which parents can switch on for a teen, stops that teen from seeing, leaving or receiving comments at all, so Bro Bros Reels aimed at older siblings should ask for a save or a share ('send this to your little brother') rather than a comment.

Instagram's 13+ teen filter hides non compliant posts in Explore, Reels, Feed, Stories and even comments from accounts a teen already follows, and teen search now blocks a wider list of mature words, so one risky stunt or rough word in a caption can hide that Reel from every teen follower even though they follow us.

Meta's 2026 teen rules restrict who sees and who can contact teens but change nothing about what adult run creator accounts may post, so for Bro Bros the risk is lost reach to teen viewers, not strikes, as long as Reels stay G rated.

The TikTok creator of the 'Apple Dance' sued Roblox in 2025 after it sold her routine as a paid emote (reportedly over 100K USD) without a signed licence, so Bro Bros should borrow a simple trend move or idea, never a creator's full signature routine step for step in a monetised video.

In Hasbro v SConnect (England and Wales High Court, judgments June and 27 Jul 2026) the Vietnamese kids channel Wolfoo was found to have copied Peppa Pig sound recordings, character voices and cheers proven by spectrogram, and the court ordered all Wolfoo videos online removed within seven days, barred future uploads across the UK, EU, US, Vietnam and other treaty countries, and opened a damages inquiry.

The Wolfoo case was won on audio alone (the look alike character claims were never needed), the studio was liable even though a contractor had added the clips before 2020, and re uploads on other channels counted as continued infringement, so for Bro Bros every sound effect, voice and cheer must be our own or properly licensed with records kept.

A court accepted a sample of 92 English Wolfoo videos as representative of a catalogue of over 30,000, so a repeated reused asset across a big kids catalogue can sink the whole library at once, not just one video.

Shorts longer than one minute are checked more strictly for music claims (Content ID can block them), which is no risk for our own Suno songs but another reason never to put any outside music, even a few seconds, in a longer Short.

YouTube began testing (Tubefilter, 3 Nov 2026) a 30 day locked period for some channels flagged under its spam policy instead of instant termination: the channel is hidden, uploads and comments are blocked, and the owner can fix or remove the flagged videos and resubmit, appeal, or delete all videos to reopen at once while keeping subscribers, handle and Partner Program status.

The spam policy's automated or synthetic mass production clause is being read as covering channels that reuse the same backing track and repeated AI imagery across many uploads, so each Bro Bros song needs its own arrangement, setting and choreography rather than one template recoloured.

Rest of World (31 Aug 2026) reports that besides Australia, Brazil and Indonesia at least 22 more countries are designing or proposing under 16 social media bans (citing an OECD blog), and that Meta paid parent influencers to promote Teen Accounts as the alternative, so more markets will push young viewers toward parent devices and kids apps.

A parent trend in November 2026 has parents filming toddlers repeating odd phrases and sounds they picked up from tablet videos, and local news coverage (KTAL, 12 Nov) tied it to YouTube's own note that not every YouTube Kids video is reviewed by hand, so Bro Bros lyrics should give children phrases parents are happy to hear repeated (please, sorry, my turn, let's try again).

A Thai cross sectional study of 214 children aged 3 to 5 (BMC Public Health, Aug 2026) found they averaged 3.0 hours of screens a day including 1.6 hours of short form video, and more short form viewing went with more inattention and hyperactive symptoms, which adds pressure on endless Shorts feeds for preschoolers and favours full songs with a clear ending.

AIR's dated 2026 policy timeline says Partner Program applications sent before 23:59 UTC on 31 Jan 2027 are still judged on today's bar (1,000 subscribers plus 4,000 watch hours in a year, or 10M Shorts views in 90 days), so Bro Bros (about 2,150 subscribers) should push long form watch hours now and apply before that cut off rather than face the doubled 8,000 hours or 20M Shorts bar.

From 1 Feb 2027 missing the deadline to accept the new Partner Program terms pauses payouts from the affected modules but does not remove a channel from the programme, so accepting the updated terms in Studio before 31 Jan 2027 is a simple must do once Bro Bros is a partner.

The 2027 programme adds a targeted Shorts ad option that pays the creator a direct 45% when an advertiser picks five channels or fewer; because made for kids ads are bought on context, not on the viewer, a clearly themed, consistent kids music channel is the kind of short list a toy or family brand could pick.

AIR's October 2026 monetisation report notes that Kids and Teens grew faster than any other of its 13 niches in September 2026, even though it keeps the lowest median RPM (about 0.33 USD), so the kids space is getting more crowded right as the high paying Q4 starts.

ClockwiseTV's CEO told Fast Company that marking videos made for kids on YouTube usually lowers AdSense income, and pitches licensing to curated ad free apps as a second income for kids creators; for Bro Bros (preschool songs) this kind of licensing deal is a later option, since ClockwiseTV itself targets ages 8 to 12 and lists no application route yet.

Ofcom says personalised feeds are the main way children meet harmful content and that YouTube and TikTok made no significant feed changes; it is investigating both, so UK rules on what kids feeds recommend may tighten, which favours calm, clearly child safe content like ours over shock thumbnails.

YouTube told Fortune (Apr 2026) that it already limits AI made content on the YouTube Kids app to a small set of high quality channels, so a new AI assisted channel like Bro Bros should expect to earn its YouTube Kids place through consistent original characters and songs rather than assume it.
YouTube also said it is building dedicated AI labels for YouTube Kids (no date given), so honest AI disclosure in our upload settings now will keep us on the right side when those labels arrive.

Fairplay estimates the top AI slop channels aimed at children earn over 4.25 million US dollars a year and that adults spot AI video only about half the time, which is why regulators and advocates keep pushing YouTube to tighten made for kids AI rules; quality and visible human craft are our long term protection.

Parents worry that December social videos showing grown ups moving the elf spoil the magic for young viewers, so Bro Bros Christmas videos should keep helpers, elves and Santa magical and never show or hint at who really moves them.

An arXiv audit (Jun 2026) of 4,208 videos from 56 kid centric family channels classed about 26.5% as exploitative and found those videos drew more views within the same channel (emotional bait about +66%, staged conflict about +40%), an association that explains why regulators and YouTube now target upsetting kids packaging; Bro Bros wins attention with surprise and fun, never fake tears or fights.

A Frontiers in Psychology mini review (Mar 2026, 10 studies of 3 to 5 year olds) found screen time linked to weaker attention mostly when viewing was passive, while active use (joining in, answering, moving) was linked to better orienting attention, which supports building every Bro Bros song around actions kids copy and questions they answer.

eSafety's three month evaluation of Australia's under 16 social media rules (more than 4,000 children aged 10 to 15 with a parent, follow up Mar to Apr 2026) found own account ownership on restricted platforms fell from about 52% to 42%, with significant drops on YouTube, Snapchat and TikTok, but more than 81% still used at least one of them, so much Australian kid viewing has moved to logged out or shared family screens where subscriptions and history do not follow the child.

In the same evaluation parents who did not know about their child's social media use rose from about 1 in 4 to about 1 in 3, most among parents of 10 to 12 year olds, while about two in three parents still back the rules; Bro Bros should keep every title, thumbnail and Short obviously preschool and parent approved so it is welcome on the family TV and in YouTube Kids.

Children in that study thought about 13.6 years is the right age for a social media account while parents said about 15.2, and messaging and gaming use rose after the rules, signs that parents, not children, increasingly choose what young kids watch, so our descriptions and channel page should speak to parents (what the song teaches, calm or active, length).

YouTube began expanding Hype with Jewels (viewer gifts during live streams) on 6 Nov 2026 to the US, Canada, the UK, Ireland, Germany, Italy, Spain, Poland and Turkey for partner channels of 500 to 500,000 subscribers, but made for kids streams have live chat and viewer gifts switched off, so our 24/7 song streams must earn from ads and watch time only.

YouTube is testing a personalised product shelf in Studio that suggests affiliate products with estimated commission (Nov 2026), but shopping features are not available on made for kids videos, so Bro Bros income plans should not count on YouTube Shopping; merchandise would need its own channel to parents.

The UAE's Federal Decree Law No. 26 of 2025 on Child Digital Safety applies to foreign platforms that target UAE users (social media, gaming, streaming), requires age checks, the strictest privacy and filtering settings on child accounts and new limits on ads aimed at young children, and bans collecting or publishing under 13 data except under set conditions, with platforms given until 31 Dec 2026 to comply, so Gulf viewing of Bro Bros will come more through supervised accounts and parent devices in 2027.

California's SB 1247 on child influencers (signed 30 Sep 2026, in force 1 Jan 2027) and AB 2246, a new Children's Design Code that replaces the old Age Appropriate Design Code, add to the wave of 2027 US state rules; because Bro Bros uses only animated characters and never films real children, the child performer rules do not touch us, which is a quiet advantage worth keeping.
leaves.src: Digital Policy Alert and Sheppard Mullin, Sep 2026

leaves.t: Australia's government said on 19 Nov 2026 it will amend its Digital Duty of Care bill so individuals can sue online platforms for breaches, aiming to pass it before Christmas; platforms like YouTube and Instagram will likely tighten what they recommend to children there, so our videos must stay clearly gentle and age appropriate.

UK lawyers note the under 16 ban's in scope test is a service built for social interaction, user posts and algorithms, with exemptions planned for education and music streaming but no final list, so it is still unknown whether kids song viewing on YouTube without an account will be touched in 2027.

The UK's 'Growing up in the online world' consultation drew over 116,000 responses and about 9 in 10 parents backed an under 16 social media ban, so parent trust signals (no comments, no data asks, calm content) will matter more for kids channels in the UK.

Al Jazeera (9 Nov 2026) reports that Meta's August 2026 settlement with US states gives under 18 Instagram users a two hour daily limit, a midnight to 6 AM curfew and no push notifications from 8 AM to 3 PM, while its AI age checks now move suspected teens into Teen Accounts worldwide, starting with Instagram, then Facebook and Threads.

Ofcom's next set of UK child safety code changes went to the government on 16 Nov 2026: services must keep illegal content out of children's recommendation feeds (for every user, or only for accounts proven to be children by strong age checks) and add reporting for livestreams showing imminent harm, so kids feeds in the UK keep getting stricter, which favours clearly safe, wholesome channels.

A 2026 Mashable report on Google's Animaj investment says the American Academy of Pediatrics advises parents to avoid AI generated video for young children and to prefer longer form shows, so Bro Bros should lead with its human made songs, consistent characters and story, and keep AI tools invisible in the result.

YouTube's five published Youth Principles say children get free access to high quality, age appropriate content, that recommendations for kids are tuned by quality principles written with child development and digital wellbeing experts, and that YouTube never shows personalised ads to children, so the safest growth path is to make every song visibly 'high quality' by those principles (a clear lesson, kindness, active movement) rather than chasing clicks.

From 1 Feb 2027 a channel already in the Partner Program also needs 10M qualified Shorts views in the last 90 days to share Shorts ad and Premium revenue; below that it keeps long form earnings and Shorts money returns automatically when it climbs back, so for Bro Bros Shorts are a discovery tool and long songs are the income.

For channels under the 10M Shorts bar YouTube promised milestone incentives in 2027 (Shopping bonuses, brand deal incentives and earnings boosts for starting and growing trends) without amounts or dates yet, so starting our own repeatable kid dance trend could later pay directly; watch for the details.

Since May 2026 YouTube automatically labels videos with significant photorealistic AI use when the creator does not disclose it, showing the label right under the player on long videos and as an overlay on Shorts, while unrealistic or animated content only gets a note in the expanded description, and YouTube says the label alone changes neither recommendations nor earnings.

YouTube makes the AI label permanent (the creator cannot remove it) for videos made with its own AI tools such as Veo or Dream Screen and for files carrying C2PA metadata that marks them as fully AI generated, so Bro Bros should export final videos from Blender without such metadata and never build scenes with Veo if we want only the quiet description note.

The same AIR report describes two Spanish kids channels that grew views by about 5x and 10x within a month after a moderation pass that removed policy risky videos and thumbnails from their catalogues, so a periodic check of our older uploads against YouTube's kids quality principles is worth doing as the library grows.

YouTube's VP of Trust and Safety (Creator Insider, Aug 2026) said the Partner Program is agnostic about which tools make a video and only restricts three kinds of AI content from earning: generic, repetitive mass produced videos that look like content farming, off putting or distressing videos such as animals in peril, and AI personas giving advice on money or other serious topics; the rule is about monetisation, not a general ban, so Suno and Meshy made songs are fine when each one is clearly its own creative piece.

Because 'animals in peril' is named as demonetisable distressing content, our animal songs should never show a pet or animal stuck, hurt or scared for drama; keep rescue or 'boo boo' care songs gentle, short on danger and quick to the happy ending.

India's amended IT Rules (in force from 20 Feb 2026) target AI made or AI altered content that looks real and could mislead: platforms must ask uploaders to declare AI generated content, verify it with their own tools, label it with a visible tag plus a permanent marker or metadata, and act on government or police takedown orders within three hours, while basic edits like cropping, colour fixes, subtitles and translation are not treated as deepfakes.

Because about 68% of our subscribers are in India, the Indian AI rules matter directly to us: clearly stylised 3D cartoon songs are low risk, but any realistic looking AI scene (a lifelike animal, a real place, a human like face) should be declared with YouTube's altered or synthetic content setting and Instagram's AI label, and we should never imitate real people or news footage.
leaves.src: Business Today, Feb 2026; Metricool (our YouTube), Nov 2026

leaves.t: Ofcom research (Mar 2026) found 72% of UK children aged 8 to 12 use apps that have a minimum age of 13, and Ofcom asked YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, Snapchat, Facebook and Roblox to report by 30 Apr 2026 on enforcing their age limits with highly effective age checks, with an assessment for Parliament due by end of October 2026 and under 16 restrictions expected from 2027; YouTube Kids has no minimum age and under 13s may use YouTube only through supervised accounts, so a growing share of our UK audience will reach us through those kid modes.
YouTube channel stands at about 2,140 subscribers with 450 to 1,400 views a day in 1 to 15 Nov 2026; the best days (10 and 12 Nov) followed the Jungle Doctors song and a Hindi Didi story.

Top long form uploads 1 to 15 Nov: Lion Needs a Doctor (833 views), Light the Diyas (783), Ek Diya Sabke Liye (456), Stomp Your Boot hoedown (382), Dhol Bajao (356), Who Took the Cookie (319): story songs with a problem to fix and festival songs lead.

Average view duration on our long form songs is only about 15 to 25 seconds; cartoon episodes hold a little longer (up to 36 s for Buddy's Birthday) but get fewer views, so early retention is our biggest weakness.
Our YouTube Shorts get almost no views (1 to 30 each) while the same moments on Instagram Reels get 50 to 125, so YouTube is not yet testing our Shorts with seed audiences.

Instagram Reels lose 58 to 90% of viewers in the first 3 seconds; the lowest skip rates were the Wave Jump Hop action song (58%), the Sports Day race (59%) and a Hindi Didi cloud story (59%), the highest were Diwali Dhamaka (90%) and Buddy's Birthday episode (88%).
Likes, comments and shares are near zero on both platforms (best: 3 shares for Jalao Deep on Instagram), so watch and skip behaviour is the only real signal we get.
Reel views were about 100 to 125 each in the first week of November but mostly 20 to 90 after 9 Nov, so Instagram reach is softening and the hook needs to improve.
Given our Shorts get almost no YouTube views, the data points to fewer, better Shorts cut fresh from each song's most energetic moment, rather than more volume.
leaves.src: Metricool Nov 2026 compared with AIR cases

leaves.t: Metricool's per video YouTube data runs about 4 days behind (on 15 Nov the newest row was the 11 Nov upload), so judge each song only after 4 or 5 days, not on its first day.

Even for an Indian festival, the English titled Diwali song Light the Diyas reached 783 views while the Hindi titled Jalao Deep rock song reached only 69, so English titles reach a wider audience for us.
Our songs outperform our cartoon episodes about 3 to 1 on views (songs mostly 100 to 830, episodes mostly 10 to 220) with similar 15 to 36 second average watch, so songs should stay the core output.

The 10 AM IST song uploads hold most of our top results (Lion Needs a Doctor, Light the Diyas, Ek Diya, Stomp Your Boot, Dhol Bajao), while 4 PM slots, often episodes, trail; content type and slot are mixed so the slot effect is not proven.

Simple sing along manner songs did modestly (Thank You 197, Zoo Stomp 102, Birthday Shake 49) compared with songs built around a small problem or mission (Lion doctor 833, Cookie mystery 319, Treasure hunt 251).
Instagram Reels posted 9 to 14 Nov got only 5 to 91 views each, down from about 100 to 125 in early November, so our Instagram reach has kept falling for two weeks.

The best Reels that week were the mystery (Who Took the Cookie, 91 views), the bedtime shy monster lullaby (65) and the pirate treasure hunt (62): a question or a little mystery in the first line pulls more viewers than an action list.

Average Reel watch time is mostly 2 to 4 seconds; the exceptions were Blast Off space bus (about 14 s), the Hindi grumpy cloud story (about 12 s) and the giant pumpkin garden song (about 9 s), all with a clear transformation (rocket launch, rain, seed to pumpkin).
Saves and shares on our Reels are still zero across the week, so nothing yet makes parents send our Reels to others, the strongest Instagram reach signal.

About 66% of our YouTube views in 1 to 15 Nov (about 9,200 of 14,000) came from Suggested videos, so being recommended next to other kids songs is our main engine; titles, thumbnails and topics should match the big channels' popular songs.
YouTube Search brought about 21% of our views (about 3,000) and subscribers only about 7%, so keyword clear titles (animal, doctor, Diwali, story song) already pay off.
The Shorts feed gave only 37 views and playlists 11 in two weeks, so our Shorts are not being tested in the feed and our playlists are almost unused as a discovery path.

Our YouTube subscribers are about 65% India and 8% US, then Pakistan (4%), Philippines (2.6%), UK (2.3%) and Bangladesh (1.6%); South Asia dominates while English songs slowly build the US and UK base.
Our scheduled YouTube posts mark 'AI generated content' as false even though the music is made in Suno; YouTube asks creators to disclose AI made music, so this setting needs a check.

Metricool reports our Instagram follower count as about 1 in Nov 2026 (worth checking in the app); if true, so every Reel view comes from non follower recommendations; growing even a few hundred followers (for example by asking parents to follow in captions and bio) would give each Reel a base audience.

Daily Instagram Reel views were about 250 to 450 from 1 to 8 Nov (3 to 5 Reels a day, Diwali season) but only about 12 to 90 from 10 to 14 Nov (2 Reels a day); views per Reel also fell, so reach dropped after the festival, not only because we posted fewer.
Average reach per Reel over 1 to 15 Nov was about 65 accounts, far below the roughly 30% reach rate typical for accounts with followers, so Instagram is still treating us as a brand new account.

Our most viewed YouTube uploads of 1 to 15 Nov were Lion Needs a Doctor (Jungle Doctors animal story song, 833 views), Light the Diyas (783), Ek Diya Sabke Liye (456), Fruit and Veggie Hoedown (382), Dhol Bajao (356) and Who Took the Cookie (319): a helper or doctor story with an animal and festival songs lead.

Our songs clearly beat our cartoon episodes: songs published 1 to 11 Nov averaged roughly 300 views each while the Bro Bros Fun episodes (Ep 12 to 18) got only 10 to 115, so the song format is what YouTube recommends for us.

Average view duration on our long songs is only about 16 to 24 seconds (Lion Needs a Doctor about 18 s), so most viewers leave in the first verse; the opening 20 seconds (hook, chorus early, a question to the child) is our biggest fix.

Each of our Shorts got 0 to 30 views (best: Diwali Time Light the Diyas, 30) while the matching long song got 50 to 800, so our Shorts are still not entering the Shorts feed; they need a stronger first second and a chorus cut, not more volume.
Metricool lists no YouTube uploads published after 11 Nov 2026 (the last was Blast Off Space Bus with 2 views), so either posting paused or syncing lags; the 14 a week schedule should be checked.
Between 1 and 14 Nov 2026 the YouTube channel went from 2,130 to 2,150 subscribers (about 1 to 2 a day, almost no losses), so growth is steady but slow.

Daily YouTube views sat at about 450 to 750 most days but jumped to 1,386 on 10 Nov and 1,296 on 12 Nov, the Diwali song days, so festival songs posted two to three days ahead roughly double our daily views.
Only 2 YouTube shares were recorded across 1 to 14 Nov, so nothing we post is yet being passed between parents; a share worthy hook (a dance challenge or a family moment) is still missing.

The 15 and 16 Nov uploads (Ant Parade, a Hindi Golu elephant story, Dooby Dooby Boom Boom, The Wiggle Bus) publish on time with a Short 5 minutes after each song and a Reel, but Reel captions still carry 7 hashtags and YouTube descriptions 10, against the finding that hashtags cut Instagram reach.
The Instagram account still shows just 1 follower in mid November 2026, so every Reel view comes from non followers and follower growth on Instagram has not started.

Instagram Reel views ran about 250 to 450 a day from 1 to 8 Nov while 3 to 5 Reels a day were posted, then fell to 12 to 153 a day from 9 to 14 Nov at 2 Reels a day (12 views on 14 Nov), so reach per Reel is tiny (often 5 to 100 people) and fewer posts did not raise it.
Reels drew only 0 to 4 interactions a day in the first half of November and no recorded shares, so no Reel has yet earned the DM sends Instagram needs to widen non follower reach.

Measured against vidIQ's medians for new channels (about 180 to 270 views in 30 days per long video), our better songs at 200 to 800 views each are above typical, while our Shorts at 0 to 30 views are far below the Shorts median of about 1,300, confirming Shorts distribution is our weakest point.

Our 12 to 15 Nov uploads keep the daily pattern (an English story song at 10 AM, a Hindi Didi story or second song at 4 PM, each with a Short 5 minutes later and a Reel), with topics garden patience, sports day kindness, bedtime monster, kitten rescue, sandcastle and ant parade, all 'made for kids' and not marked AI generated.

Metricool's best time to post model for our brand (IST, 16 to 22 Nov 2026) shows YouTube's two weekday peaks at 10:00 and 16:00, with 16:00 the strongest hour every weekday (top value Wednesday 16:00) and Saturday and Sunday at roughly half the weekday level, so our 10 AM and 4 PM upload slots match the model.

For Instagram the same model peaks at 10:00 IST (Wed to Fri strongest) with a second rise at 18:00, while 15:00 to 16:00 is a dip, so moving the afternoon Reel from 4 PM to about 6 PM IST is a cheap test.

Because the biggest kids song brand uses Instagram to talk to parents (relatable parenting jokes, behind the scenes, movie news) rather than to toddlers, Bro Bros Reels should mix song clips with parent facing hooks ('when your kid asks for this song 40 times').

A karaoke lyric line (each word lights up as it is sung, big rounded font in the lower middle, inside the TV safe zone) should be the default on Bro Bros singalong uploads, because captions lift co viewing and also help English learners worldwide.

For Bro Bros compilations the evidence now points to about 20 to 40 minute mixes of proven songs for normal uploads, with very long content kept for 24/7 live streams rather than 3 hour uploads, which YouTube stopped favouring in 2025.
leaves.src: Little Dot and AIR stream data, 2026

leaves.t: For Bro Bros long compilations, titles can borrow the parent search pattern of Ms Rachel and the two hook stack of Cocomelon, for example 'Toddler Dance Party: Learn to Count + Freeze Dance | Bro Bros Fun', instead of only a song name.

Because Australia, New Zealand and Canada pay among the highest RPMs, a southern hemisphere summer Christmas song and a Canadian snow song are worth making even though those audiences are smaller than India or Indonesia.

To be ready for cut testing, every major Bro Bros song should keep two alternative openings in the Blender project (one starting on the dance hook, one on a funny moment), costing little extra render time.

So one Bro Bros song needs two vertical cuts: a 20 to 30 second YouTube Short built around the chorus and dance hook, and a fuller 45 to 60 second Instagram Reel with verse plus chorus, rather than posting the identical clip on both.

The scheduled week of 16 to 22 Nov 2026 holds 14 English songs (Dooby Dooby Boom Boom, Wiggle Bus, Digger, Boo Boo Bandage, Veggie Kitchen, Freeze Arcade, Farm Band, Circus Parade, Car Safety, Kitty Band, Toothbrushing, Peekaboo, Rocket, Bubble Gum Beach), each with a Short 5 minutes later and a Reel, but none uses a December holiday theme or a trend bank format while holiday Reels are already peaking.

No Hindi Didi story is scheduled for 16 to 22 Nov, although on Instagram the Didi stories held viewers longest in 9 to 14 Nov (about 4 to 12 seconds average watch against about 2 to 4 seconds for most English song Reels), so dropping them removes our best Reel retention format.

Rockets and space have now appeared three times in three weeks (Rocket Ride 5 Nov, Blast Off Space Bus 11 Nov with only 2 YouTube views by Metricool's last sync, and a rocket song on 22 Nov), and tooth brushing twice (4 and 21 Nov); repeating a winner is fine, but near repeats of weak performers add to the template feel YouTube's inauthentic content checks look for.
Metricool's YouTube data for our channel still stops at uploads of 11 Nov 2026 on 16 Nov, so YouTube results for the last five days cannot yet be judged; Instagram data is current.

The 13 Nov 2026 bedtime Reel (a shy fluffy monster afraid of the dark) reached 65 views, three times the other story songs of 12 to 14 Nov, which supports keeping one calm bedtime song in each week's mix.

The same sports day topic drew 110 Reel views on 8 Nov as a cartoon clip but only 21 on 13 Nov as a story song, so the late November slump is mostly lower account distribution, and a hook in the first second (speech plus a face) matters more than topic choice right now.

Reels posted on 14 Nov 2026 (sandcastle and kitten rescue story songs) had only 5 and 7 views after a day, the lowest of the month, so the next scheduled week should test trend bank formats and a Hindi Didi story Reel to break the slide.

On 16 Nov 2026 (about 02:40 IST) Metricool still has YouTube stats only for uploads up to 11 Nov and Instagram Reels stats only up to 14 Nov, so the 15 Nov Ant Parade song and Golu elephant Didi story cannot be judged yet; the YouTube sync gap is now five days.

Our Boo Boo Bandage song (scheduled 17 Nov 2026, 4 PM IST) follows BabyBus's 'Boo Boo Song, Ouchie Ouchie' upload of 12 Nov, which confirms boo boo care as a live topic but puts us beside a 44M subscriber channel in search, so our title and thumbnail should lean on our own hook (the toy clinic, Teddy's paw) rather than the generic 'boo boo song' phrase.

A Hindi Didi story Reel (Golu the elephant's giant sneeze) did go out on 15 Nov 2026 at 4 PM IST, so our best retaining Reel format is still running this week even though the 16 to 22 Nov plan is mostly English songs.

Measured against vidIQ's new channel norm of about 1,360 views per Short, our Shorts at 0 to 30 views are roughly 50 times lower, so the problem is how our Shorts are made and set up (a trimmed piece of the long song, posted five minutes after it, made for kids) rather than channel age; the next test should be Shorts built as standalone hooks (a trend format or a question in the first second).

Metricool's YouTube sync now reaches 13 Nov 2026: daily views were about 1,386 on 10 Nov, 914 on 11 Nov, 1,296 on 12 Nov and 1,055 on 13 Nov, roughly double the 450 to 750 a day of 2 to 8 Nov, and subscribers rose from about 2,130 to 2,150 by 15 Nov (about 1 to 5 gained a day).

Instagram posted 4 to 5 Reels a day from 2 to 7 Nov 2026 (daily Reel views about 250 to 415, daily reach about 60 to 88) but only 2 a day from 9 to 15 Nov, when daily Reel views fell to about 25 to 153 and reach to about 10 to 49; halving the number of Reels coincided with a drop of roughly 70% in views.

Our Instagram account still shows about 1 follower in Metricool while Reels reach 10 to 90 people a day, so almost all Instagram views come from non followers; captions, the first second and shareable moments, not follower counts, decide our Reels reach for now.

The 15 Nov 2026 Ant Parade Reel (tiny ants marching off with a cookie, a 'left, right' chant, then the Bros share their picnic) reached 113 views and 88 people with a 74% skip rate, our best Reel since the 9 Nov cookie mystery (91 views), so marching chants with a small cheeky animal problem work on Instagram.

The 15 Nov Hindi Didi story Reel (Golu the elephant's giant sneeze) got only 9 views with an 89% skip rate, the weakest of the week, so the earlier idea that Didi stories are our best retaining Reel format no longer holds.

Across 9 to 15 Nov 2026 our 10 English story song Reels averaged about 43 views each and our 4 Hindi Didi story Reels about 22, so on Instagram the English songs now pull about twice the views of the Hindi stories.
Both top Reels of the week (cookie mystery 91 views, ant parade 113) involve food being taken and then shared, which suggests a 'who took the snack?' hook is our most reliable Reel opener so far.

Lesson from Cartoon Clubhouse and Pancake Manor: judge a new Bro Bros song on its views after several months, not its first week, and give each proven song a second life as an on screen lyric sing along version inside a longer compilation.

leaves.t: For Bro Bros Reels, once one story song Reel clearly beats the rest (Ant Parade at 113 views so far), the next Reels should copy its exact opening structure (food taken, a chant, sharing) with new animals and foods, and the best one should be re posted as a Trial Reel with a new first second rather than left alone.

leaves.t: The 'something got taken, who did it?' hook now has three independent wins: our cookie mystery and ant parade Reels were our best of the week, and a German movement channel's two all time top songs are a stolen cookie and a lost dog bone, so a missing snack or toy mystery should be a regular Bro Bros format.
leaves.src: own synthesis of vidIQ and Metricool data, Nov 2026

leaves.t: Across our 42 Instagram Reels from 2 to 15 Nov 2026 the 3 second skip rate (40 to 100%) had almost no link to views (correlation about 0.04): Birthday Shake had 121 views with an 85% skip rate while the sandcastle story had 18 views with 100%, so with so few views per Reel, skip rate alone is not yet a reliable guide and total views plus reach should decide which hooks to repeat.

On Instagram our cartoon episode clips (Zoomy, treasure hunt, guess the sound, pressure cooker) averaged about 92 views in 2 to 8 Nov, the same as our song Reels (about 94), even though on YouTube our songs beat episodes about 3 to 1, so short funny episode moments still deserve Reel slots while YouTube long form stays song first.

vidIQ's July 2026 benchmarks give channels with 1,000 to 9,999 subscribers a median growth of about 0.51% a month (about 13 subscribers); our channel rose from about 2,130 to 2,150 subscribers in roughly a week in mid November, about 1% a week or several times the median, so the channel is growing faster than most of its size even while views per video are small.
leaves.src: vidIQ Research, Jul 2026, and Metricool (our data), Nov 2026

leaves.t: With one Short published 5 minutes after every song, about half of our YouTube uploads are Shorts, above AIR's 25 to 40% sweet spot and close to the 55% level where results weaken, and our Shorts get almost no views, so trimming to Shorts only for the best one or two songs a day (about 25 to 35% of uploads) fits both the data and our own results; the change should be made once and kept, since mid year strategy swings did worst.
leaves.src: own synthesis of AIR study and Metricool (our data), Nov 2026

leaves.t: All 18 posts scheduled for 16 to 18 Nov 2026 (6 songs, each as a long video, a Short and a Reel) have YouTube 'isAiGeneratedContent' and Instagram 'isAiGenerated' set to false even though the music comes from Suno; YouTube says the disclosure does not change recommendations or monetisation for animated content, so turning it on for the long videos is a free safeguard as AI scrutiny of kids content grows.

The six songs going out 16 to 18 Nov (drum clap stomp freeze, Wiggle Bus, Dig Dig Digger, Boo Boo Bandage, Roly Poly Tomato tango, Freeze Arena) all match the playbook (action verbs, vehicles, care routines, freeze games, timestamped descriptions), but none is wintry or Christmas themed even though big channels start holiday uploads in the second half of November, so the next week should bring winter and Christmas songs forward.

Two of the six songs scheduled 16 to 18 Nov are freeze dance songs (the drum song's statue freeze and the Freeze Arena), two days apart; freeze games are proven, but spacing look alike formats at least a week apart and giving each a clearly different hook protects us from YouTube's repetitive content checks.

With YouTube data now reaching 15 Nov 2026, the Giant Pumpkin garden story song (12 Nov) is our most viewed long video of the fortnight at 924 views, ahead of Jungle Doctors (858), Space Bus (554) and The Big Race (515), so a magic growing garden topic is now our strongest English song.

Across 9 to 14 Nov the six 10 AM IST English story songs averaged about 575 YouTube views each against about 280 for the six 4 PM uploads (three Hindi Didi stories and three English songs), so the content and language of the slot matter more than the 4 PM hour that Metricool's model rates highest.

The 14 Nov 4 PM beach song (Sandcastle vs The Wave) has only 76 YouTube views after two days, our weakest English song of the week, while the same day's 10 AM kitten rescue reached 330, which hints that a seasonal mismatch (a beach topic in a northern winter week) costs views.

Our Instagram Reels averaged about 86 views each in 2 to 8 Nov 2026 (Diwali, Zoomy episode clips and action songs) but only about 43 for the English story song Reels of 9 to 15 Nov, so reach halved once we switched to a single story song format; the format change and post Diwali dip both likely played a part.

In 9 to 15 Nov the best Instagram Reels were the Ant Parade marching song (113 views, 15 Nov) and the Detective Bros cookie mystery (91 views), both with a clear repeated action or a question to solve, while the sandcastle (18) and kitten rescue (7) Reels nearly flopped.

Our four Hindi Didi story Reels of 10 to 15 Nov averaged only about 22 views each (the 15 Nov sneezing elephant story got 9) against about 43 for English song Reels the same week, even though they hold viewers longer, so on our mainly English account the Hindi stories reach few new people.

All eight songs queued for 19 to 22 Nov 2026 (farm band, bubble gum, elephant parade, little car, kitty band, tooth brushing, peekaboo, ride to the moon) are evergreen, so Bro Bros will reach 23 Nov with no winter or Christmas song while Spotify's holiday listening has been running since late October; the first festive songs should be in the week of 23 Nov.

The 20 Nov 10 AM Elephant Stomp Parade song lands six days before the 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade (26 Nov) and matches the rising one by one parade format, so its Reel and Short can be cut as animals marching past the camera one at a time to ride both.

The 21 Nov tooth brushing song repeats a topic we already posted on 4 Nov (Brush Brush Brush Reel, 72 views), so it is worth giving it a clearly different hook (the giant bathroom and sugar bugs) in the title and first second rather than another 'brush brush' opening.

Our 42 posts queued for 16 to 22 Nov 2026 follow one fixed pattern for each of the 14 songs (YouTube long video at 10 AM or 4 PM IST, its Short at five past, and the Instagram Reel at the same hour); the 17 Nov 'Boo boo bandage' toy clinic song matches a proven topic (Little Angel's boo boo care song has about 63M views), while the 18 Nov neon freeze dance is the only song with even a snowflake hint, so no Christmas or winter song is scheduled before 23 Nov.

Across our 42 Instagram Reels of 2 to 15 Nov 2026 the skip rate (viewers gone before 3 seconds) averaged about 73 to 77% for every format (songs, Zoomy episode clips, English story songs, Hindi Didi stories) and had almost no link to views, so three in four viewers leave in the first 3 seconds whatever we post; the opening frame and first sound, not the format, are our biggest Reel weakness.

Our powerful Diwali rock song Reel (8 Nov, dhol, guitars and fireworks) held an average of about 20 seconds per view on 115 views, five times our usual 3 to 5 seconds, and the Space Bus story song (11 Nov) held about 14 seconds, so a loud, high energy musical opening with an instant countdown or drum hit is the pattern that keeps Reel viewers watching.

Zoomy episode clips and action songs averaged about 82 to 88 views per Reel in early November against about 43 for English story songs and 22 for Hindi Didi stories, yet the Didi stories had the lowest skip rate (about 71%) and the longest watch (about 6 seconds), so Didi stories win attention once seen but are rarely shown, a distribution problem that captions and a clearer first frame should address before dropping the format.

Of about 16,900 YouTube views from 2 to 16 Nov 2026, 71% came from Suggested (next to other videos), 17% from YouTube search, 6% from subscribers, 3% from our channel page and only 0.3% from the Shorts feed and 0.1% from playlists, so Bro Bros lives on Suggested and search; titles that match what parents type and end screens that chain our own songs matter far more than Shorts as a traffic source right now.

Playlists brought only 12 of about 16,900 YouTube views in the first half of November and the Shorts feed only 48, so our playlists are not yet being surfaced and our Shorts are not sending viewers on to full songs; themed playlists (bath and bedtime, vehicles, winter) set as the end screen target and a related video link on every Short are the two cheapest fixes to test.

Between 10 and 14 Nov 2026 about 87 to 94% of our daily YouTube views (for example 1,296 of 1,386 on 10 Nov) went to videos published since 3 Nov, so songs older than about a week bring almost no views; each new song gets roughly one week of life unless a playlist, compilation or end screen keeps sending viewers back to it.

Daily YouTube views climbed from about 450 to 500 a day (3 to 6 Nov) to 900 to 1,400 (10 to 13 Nov) while uploads stayed at 3 to 4 a day, then eased to about 850 on 14 Nov, so the second week of November lifted the whole channel and the next check should see whether this holds or fades with the newer songs.

Our YouTube channel averaged about 1,080 views a day from 11 to 15 Nov 2026 against about 730 a day from 4 to 10 Nov (+49%), and Sunday 15 Nov drew 1,301 views from only two uploads, so view growth is holding even on lighter upload days; Metricool has no YouTube data after 15 Nov yet.

Subscribers moved only from about 2,130 to 2,150 between 4 and 15 Nov 2026 (1 to 5 gained a day while 450 to 1,400 views a day came in), roughly one new subscriber per 500 views, so our viewers watch via Suggested without subscribing and each song needs a sung or visual 'come back for more' moment at the end.

Our Instagram Reels earned about 250 to 415 views a day on 4 to 8 Nov (3 to 5 Reels a day, about 80 views each) but only about 25 to 150 a day on 10 to 17 Nov (2 Reels a day, about 30 views each; 16 and 17 Nov brought 44 and 38 views), and the account still shows 1 follower, so Instagram is not yet pushing our Reels beyond a small test audience.

Metricool's YouTube data now reaches 16 Nov 2026: 858 views that day with 0 new subscribers (after 1,301 views on 15 Nov), and subscribers have stayed at 2,150 from 14 to 18 Nov, so views hold near 1,000 a day while subscriber growth has stalled.

From 13 to 16 Nov our YouTube views averaged about 1,016 a day (1,055, 850, 1,301, 858) against vidIQ's median of about 234 first week views per long video, so our new videos together already beat a typical single upload, but none has broken out yet.

Metricool's YouTube data still stops at 16 Nov 2026 on 19 Nov (subscribers 2,150; 12 to 16 Nov views 1,296, 1,055, 850, 1,301 and 858), so there is still nothing new to judge songs or slots by until the feed catches up.

On 18 Nov 2026 both Bro Bros Reels passed 100 views again (veggie soup song 127 at 10:02 IST, freeze dance 111 at 16:02 IST) after 10 to 17 Nov when most Reels got only 7 to 33 views, so the Instagram dip was temporary rather than a lasting penalty.

Both of our 18 Nov Reels that recovered open with a playful game cue in the caption and the clip ('Uh oh, the tomato rolled... catch it!' and 'Dance dance dance... FREEZE!'), while calmer story Reels (sandcastle 18 views, kitten rescue 7, boo boo bandage 13) stayed low, so game and action hooks suit Reels better than story songs.

A high 3 second view rate did not bring reach on its own: the digger Reel on 17 Nov had our best view rate (63%, skip rate 37%) yet only 31 views, while the 18 Nov Reels with 66 to 75% skip rates reached over 100, so Instagram's push depends on more than the first seconds (shares, watch time and timing also count).

Our longest average Reel watch times since 5 Nov were the Diwali rock song (20.3 seconds, 115 views), the space bus song (13.9 s) and the Hindi rain cloud story (11.7 s), while most Reels hold only 2 to 5 seconds, so loud festival energy and strong music keep Instagram viewers far longer than our usual clips.
Metricool's YouTube feed still stops at 16 Nov 2026 when checked on 19 Nov at 09:40 IST (subscribers 2,150, 858 views on 16 Nov), so YouTube song and slot comparisons for 17 and 18 Nov must wait.

AIR Media-Tech's YouTube Kids access service accepts channels from 1,500 subscribers; Bro Bros has about 2,150, so we already qualify to have an official YouTube partner submit us for YouTube Kids review, which creators cannot do alone.

Our Metricool queue for 19 to 22 Nov 2026 still publishes at 10:00 and 16:00 IST (long video and Reel at the same minute, its Short 5 minutes later), not the plan's 16:00 plus 04:30 IST, so the US after school test has not started; nothing is queued yet from 23 Nov, the natural point to switch the 10:00 slot to 04:30 IST.

Every Bro Bros description promises 'New songs every day at 10 AM and 4 PM', so if the morning slot moves to 04:30 IST the description line should change to something time free such as 'New songs every day!' to avoid a broken promise for viewers outside India.

This week's queued songs (farm band, bubble gum pop, elephant parade, little car, kitty band, toothbrushing, peekaboo hide and seek, rocket to the moon) all have timestamps, a 'Kids learn' line and made for kids set, matching the playbook; none is a seasonal winter or Christmas song yet, though competitors posted theirs from 16 Nov.

Metricool's YouTube feed for Bro Bros still ended at 16 Nov when checked at 11:50 IST on 19 Nov (2,150 subscribers, about 850 to 1,300 views a day from 12 to 16 Nov), so the YouTube side of this week's songs cannot be judged yet.

Against that benchmark our Reels from 17 and 18 Nov 2026 open poorly: the freeze dance (66% skip), veggie soup (75%) and boo boo bandage (77%) Reels lose about three in four viewers in the first 3 seconds and only the digger Reel (37%) is near average, so the first second of every Reel should start mid dance or mid action with the song's hook, not an intro shot.
leaves.src: Metricool (Bro Bros Instagram), Nov 2026; CreatorStack benchmark

leaves.t: Metricool shows the 19 Nov 2026 16:00 IST long video 'Bubble Gum Pop' went live on YouTube with a warning, 'Could not upload video thumbnail', so it is running on an automatic frame instead of our designed thumbnail; the owner should set the thumbnail by hand in YouTube Studio and check every Metricool post for this warning, because a missing custom thumbnail can cut click rate on Home and Suggested.

Everything else in this week's queue (farm band at 10:00, the 10:05 Shorts, the 10:00 and 16:00 Reels) published normally on 19 Nov, and the rest of the week (elephant parade, little car, kitty band, toothbrushing, peekaboo, rocket to the moon) is still queued at 10:00 and 16:00 IST with made for kids set.

At 21:47 IST on 19 Nov 2026 the Metricool queue held 18 posts for 20 to 22 Nov (elephant parade, little car, kitty band, toothbrushing, peekaboo, ride to the moon at 10:00 and 16:00 IST) and nothing after 22 Nov 16:05 IST, so next week's 14 songs still need to be queued before Monday 23 Nov.

Metricool's YouTube feed for Bro Bros (checked 21:50 IST, 19 Nov 2026) shows about 10.9K views across 5 to 16 Nov (about 900 a day, best days 10 Nov 1,386 and 15 Nov 1,301, lowest 6 Nov 448) and subscribers rising from 2,130 to 2,150 with 20 gained and 2 lost; view data still stops at 16 Nov, so this week's songs cannot be judged yet.

Our two 18 Nov 2026 Reels held viewers only about 4.2 to 4.5 seconds on average (veggie soup 127 views, 1 share; freeze dance 111 views), and Metricool had not yet synced any 19 Nov Reel by 21:50 IST, so the first 3 seconds remain our biggest Instagram problem.

Across our ten Reels of 14 to 18 Nov 2026, the five posted at 10:00 IST averaged about 60 views (median 31) and the five posted at 16:00 IST about 36 (median 18), so the morning Reel slot is ahead on Instagram, matching Metricool's own Instagram peak at 10:00 and its afternoon dip.

Our best Reels of 14 to 18 Nov drew only about 1.1 to 1.3 views per person reached (freeze dance 111 views from 95 people, veggie soup 127 from 110, ant parade 114 from 89), so viewers almost never replay them; a seamless loop ending that runs straight back into the opening chant is the cheapest fix to test.

At about 04:40 IST on 20 Nov 2026 Metricool still showed no Reel after 18 Nov and YouTube views only up to 16 Nov (2,150 subscribers), so the 19 Nov uploads, including Bubble Gum Pop with its missing thumbnail, still cannot be judged.

Against Metricool's 2026 average (61% of organic views from the Shorts feed) Bro Bros got only about 0.3% of views from the Shorts feed in 2 to 16 Nov, so our Shorts are barely being shown at all; making Shorts as their own stand alone pieces is our largest untapped source of views.

Our 19 Nov 2026 Reels synced to Metricool by 07:40 IST on 20 Nov and are the weakest start so far: the farm animal band Reel (10:00 IST) had 4 views from 4 people with 75% skipping in the first 3 seconds, and Bubble Gum Pop (16:00 IST) 9 views with 89% skipping and about 2.3 seconds watched.

Our 16:00 IST Reels are stalling: the 17 Nov boo boo bandage Reel has only 13 views after three days and Bubble Gum Pop 9 after a day, while the 10:00 IST Reels of 17 and 18 Nov reached 31 and 127, so the morning Reel slot keeps winning on Instagram.

Metricool's YouTube data now runs to 17 Nov 2026: about 1,036 views that day, and subscribers sat at 2,150 all week with only 6 gained and none lost from 14 to 17 Nov, so our long videos hold steady daily views but are not yet converting viewers into subscribers.

Today's 20 Nov 10:00 IST long video, Elephant Stomp Parade, also went live with Metricool's 'Could not upload video thumbnail' warning, the second of our last three long videos (after Bubble Gum Pop) running on an automatic frame, so the owner should set both thumbnails by hand in YouTube Studio and upload thumbnails directly there until Metricool's thumbnail step is fixed.

With YouTube data now reaching 18 Nov 2026, Roly Poly Red Tomato (18 Nov 10:00 IST) already had 494 views, far ahead of the same week's Wiggle Bus (251), Boo Boo Bandage (177) and Dig Dig Digger (60), so a playful food and cooking game song is our strongest English start of the week and deserves a follow up (a fruit salad or pizza making song).

Our Hindi Didi story long videos are remarkably steady: four of the five from 10 to 15 Nov 2026 sit at 456 to 466 views each (magic pencil, sulky cloud, elephant sneeze), close to our best English songs, so one Hindi story a day is a reliable base audience worth keeping alongside the English songs.

Among our YouTube Shorts of 6 to 17 Nov 2026 the only ones above 15 views are Hindi (elephant sneeze Short 20, Diwali dhol and rock Shorts 20 each), while English song Shorts stay at 1 to 12 views, so Hindi Shorts find a feed audience more easily and are a cheap test for more Shorts reach.

Our 18 Nov 2026 freeze dance Reel, posted in the 16:00 IST slot, reached 113 views from 96 people with the lowest skip rate of the week (66%) and about 4.5 seconds average watch, almost level with the 10:00 IST tomato Reel (127), so the weak 16:00 Reels (boo boo bandage 13, bubble gum 9) failed on their hook, not on the hour.

Across our six Reels of 17 to 19 Nov 2026 the two that passed 100 views were movement games with an instant action in the caption's first words (roll and catch the tomato, dance then FREEZE), while care, band and bubble themes stayed under 35, so game style songs should lead our Reels.

None of our 17 to 19 Nov Reels has a single save and only two have one share each, so on Instagram we are not yet giving parents a reason to keep or send a Reel; a short on screen line such as 'save this for your next rainy day dance' is worth testing.

Because TV co views now inflate public view counts and watch time from 16 Nov 2026 (on top of every Short start counting as a view), compare Bro Bros songs week to week on engaged views, unique viewers, the co view rate and RPM in YouTube Studio, not the public counter, and mark 16 Nov as a break in our view history.

The 20 Nov 2026 16:00 IST long video 'Beep Beep Little Car' and its Short and Reel all published cleanly with the designed thumbnail (no warning), so the thumbnail failure hit two of the last four long videos (Bubble Gum Pop, Elephant Stomp Parade) rather than every upload; a manual thumbnail upload in YouTube Studio fixes those two.

Across our nine long videos of 14 to 18 Nov 2026 the average view lasted only about 11 to 20 seconds; story songs held longest (picnic ant parade, Hindi elephant sneeze, sandcastle vs the wave, about 20 s each) and the digger construction song shortest (about 11 s), so the first 20 seconds of every song need a story hook (a problem to solve) rather than a long intro.

More than a day after posting, our 19 Nov 2026 Reels were still at 9 views (Bubble Gum Beach, 89% skipped in the first 3 seconds) and 4 views (farm animal band, 75% skipped), confirming that a Reel which opens slowly gets no late pickup; the two 18 Nov Reels that opened on an instant action passed 110 views each.

Metricool now shows 18 Nov 2026 for our YouTube channel (984 views, no new subscribers), so from 14 to 18 Nov we averaged about 1,000 views a day but gained only 6 subscribers in five days, which means views are not yet turning into subscribers and an end screen or subscribe moment in each song is worth testing.

By 21 Nov 2026 Roly Poly Red Tomato (18 Nov, 10:00 IST) had 972 views, almost double its 494 two days earlier and about 3 times the week's next best (Boo Boo Bandage 288), so a funny food character that rolls away and must be caught is our clearest early hit and deserves a sequel and a place at the top of the next compilation.

Our Shorts from 17 and 18 Nov 2026 have only 3 to 7 views each days after posting, while their long versions reached 48 to 972, so Shorts posted 5 minutes after the long video are getting almost no Shorts feed reach and the planned test of a different Short timing or a stronger first second hook is now urgent.
